questions.stimulusText:
Consider a signaling system in which one brief flash means OPEN and one long flash means CLOSED. A disturbed signal might turn a brief flash into a long one, changing the message completely. One way to protect the message is to send each flash three times.
The receiver follows a majority rule: whichever kind of flash appears at least twice determines the message. Suppose the sender transmits three brief flashes, but a disturbance changes one into a long flash. The receiver still observes two brief flashes and correctly reads OPEN. The repeated information provides a backup.
This protection has limits. If two of the three brief flashes change, the receiver observes two long flashes and reads CLOSED. The rule still produces a decision, but that decision is wrong. A disagreement among the received flashes shows that something changed; it does not by itself reveal how many flashes changed.
Repetition also creates overhead: transmitting one message requires three flashes instead of one. The receiver gains protection against a single changed flash at the cost of extra signaling. Whether this trade-off is useful depends on the importance of the message and the likelihood of disturbances. More repetition is therefore a design choice, rather than an automatic improvement in every situation.

questions.stimulusText:
Imagine a painting made of a gray rectangle crossed by an orange arc. Without a title, a viewer might see a doorway, a road, or simply two shapes. Add the title Harbor at Noon, and the same marks may suggest a pier and sunlight on water. The paint has not changed, but the viewer's starting point has.
A title can offer a direction without supplying a complete route. It may name a subject, suggest a mood, or invite a question. A title such as Return does not identify who is returning or whether the return is welcome. Its usefulness may lie precisely in the questions it leaves open.
Titles can also acquire an authority they do not deserve. Suppose the artist explains that Harbor at Noon was chosen after the painting was finished. The title still belongs to the work, but it is not evidence that the orange arc was planned as sunlight. Viewers who treat it as a strict set of instructions may overlook other relationships among the shapes.
Refusing to read titles would discard a useful part of the encounter. Treating them as final answers would narrow it. A title is most productive when it enters into conversation with what a viewer notices, rather than replacing the act of looking.

questions.stimulusText:
My brother Soren was arranging pale stones in a spiral on the wet sand. He had spent the morning carrying them from the foot of the dunes, choosing each one for its color. The first curve was wide enough to step inside; the final stones crowded around a dark pebble at the center.
I watched a thin sheet of water creep toward the outer ring. "You should have built it higher up," I said. "The tide will take it."
Soren pressed one last stone into place. "I know."
I reached for a flat stone that had begun to rock in the wash. He caught my wrist gently, then let go. "Watch this part."
The water unstitched the spiral one stone at a time. A curve broke into a dotted line. The dotted line became a scattering. I expected Soren to turn away, but he crouched beside me as if something important had just begun.
For a moment the dark center remained, surrounded by tiny bubbles. Then a wave covered it too. I could no longer point to where the spiral had ended.
On the walk back, I asked whether he would make another tomorrow.
"Different stones," he said. "A different tide."
I stopped looking over my shoulder for what was gone.

My brother Soren was arranging pale stones in a spiral on the wet sand. He had spent the morning carrying them from the foot of the dunes, choosing each one for its color. The first curve was wide enough to step inside; the final stones crowded around a dark pebble at the center.

Soren pressed one last stone into place. "I know."
I reached for a flat stone that had begun to rock in the wash. He caught my wrist gently, then let go. "Watch this part."

questions.stimulusTitle: Why a Bridge Needs Room to Move
questions.stimulusText:
A bridge can look motionless while its materials slowly change size. Metal generally expands as it warms and contracts as it cools. Over the length of a bridge, many tiny changes can add up to noticeable movement. A design that allows no room for this movement can place stress on its parts.
Many bridges therefore include expansion joints: controlled gaps between sections or where the deck meets an approach. A joint may contain sliding metal pieces or flexible material. Its purpose is not to hold the gap at one width. Instead, it permits the gap to narrow or widen while keeping the crossing usable.
The amount of travel allowed by a joint depends on several things, including the length of the bridge section, the material, and the temperatures expected at the site. A longer section usually requires more room for temperature-related movement than a shorter section made from the same material under the same conditions.
The gap also needs attention after construction. Sand or small stones can collect inside it and restrict movement. Inspectors therefore check whether joints remain clear and whether their moving parts still function. A useful gap is not simply an empty space left by accident; it is a working feature whose freedom to change must be preserved.

questions.stimulusText:
In a round-robin contest, each participant plays every other participant once. Suppose the rules award one point for a win and no points for a loss, with no tied games. Playing all opponents gives each participant the same number of opportunities to earn points. It does not guarantee a single participant will finish ahead of everyone else.
Consider three players, Aster, Bram, and Cleo. Aster defeats Bram, Bram defeats Cleo, and Cleo defeats Aster. Each finishes with one win and one loss. Their results form a circle rather than a simple ranking from strongest to weakest.
A rule that breaks a tie by comparing the tied players' results against one another cannot separate these three: those are exactly the results that produced the tie. The organizers would need another rule, perhaps comparing points scored within games or arranging an extra contest. Either method must be announced clearly so that participants know what will count.
Round-robin play is therefore a way to collect results, not a promise that the results will settle every question. Organizers must distinguish between giving everyone an equal schedule and deciding what to do when that schedule produces equal totals. The format answers who will meet whom; additional rules may still be needed to turn the record into final standings.

At eleven-forty, my uncle set another carton beside my chair. "Good thing you're here for the afternoon," he said. "Della can finish the lettering while you sort these."

Rain had canceled the afternoon outside, so Tavi agreed to play hide-and-seek with his little cousin Benji. He counted slowly in the hallway, with both hands over his eyes, while a chair scraped across the sitting-room floor.
When Tavi entered, a blue sock protruded from beneath the tablecloth. The rest of Benji was hidden behind a chair. Tavi had been ready to announce his discovery immediately. Then the sock went perfectly still, and he heard a small breath being held.
"This will require a very careful search," Tavi said.
He wore a solemn expression as he examined the empty umbrella stand. He looked behind a cushion too thin to hide a kitten. Under the table, the blue sock trembled. A giggle escaped, followed by a louder cough meant to cover it.
"Nothing here," Tavi announced to the ceiling.
At last, he knelt beside the table and lifted one corner of the cloth. Benji burst out before Tavi could say a word.
"You nearly didn't find me!"
"Nearly," Tavi agreed.
Benji ran into the hallway to count. Tavi stood for a moment beside the umbrella stand. Instead of choosing the narrow cupboard he had already considered, he settled behind the sofa and left the toe of one shoe in view.

questions.stimulusText:
People often say that suction pulls a drink up a straw. That phrase describes what the action feels like, but pressure provides a fuller explanation. In an open cup, the liquid's surface is exposed to the surrounding air. Removing some air from the straw lowers the pressure inside it. The greater pressure outside can then push liquid upward through the tube.
As the liquid rises, it forms a column with weight. Supporting a taller column requires a greater pressure difference than supporting a shorter column of the same liquid. Since the pressure inside cannot be reduced without limit, a straw cannot lift liquid to any height merely by being made longer.
A leak above the liquid can interfere with the process. Air entering through the leak reduces the pressure difference that supports the column. A small leak does not always stop the liquid completely: the result depends on how quickly air enters compared with how quickly it is removed. A larger opening can make a useful pressure difference much harder to maintain.
The tube, then, is not simply a pathway that attracts liquid. It helps separate regions of different pressure. Its height and any openings in its wall matter because they affect the conditions that allow the surrounding air to push the liquid upward.

questions.stimulusTitle: Not All Light Reaches the Eye
questions.stimulusText:
A red tile does not send red light into the eye under every possible lamp. Its appearance depends both on the light reaching it and on which parts of that light the surface reflects. Consider an idealized tile that does not glow and reflects only red light. White light contains a mixture of colors. Under white illumination, this tile reflects the red component and absorbs the others, so it looks red.
Now replace the white lamp with one that supplies only blue light. There is no red component for the tile to reflect. The tile therefore looks very dark. An ideal white tile, which reflects all the visible colors reaching it, looks blue under that same blue lamp. The materials have not changed; the available illumination has.
A filter adds another selective step. It transmits certain colors and blocks others. A red-only filter cannot turn blue light into red light: if only blue light reaches it, no light passes through. A filter may be placed before the tile or between the tile and the observer's eye.
Ordinary surfaces and filters are not such perfect selectors, so actual contrasts may be less absolute. Still, appearance depends on the light that survives the whole path from source to surface to eye.

questions.stimulusText:
When a ribbon is cut at a new building's entrance, the scissors do not finish the roof or make the stairs safe. Workers have already completed those tasks. Yet the ribbon cutting can mark the beginning of public use. It gives a visible form to a change that construction work alone does not announce to everyone at once.
A graduation ceremony has a comparable role. The learning recognized there took place over months or years. Walking across a platform does not create that earlier learning. It brings people together to acknowledge it. Someone unable to attend has not therefore lost the knowledge gained beforehand.
Calling such actions empty because they do not perform the underlying work overlooks their public function. A ceremony can provide a shared signal: now this place is open, or now this achievement is being recognized. Its participants can understand a transition together rather than discover it separately.
Ceremonies are punctuation in a shared story. They do not supply all the words, but they help a group recognize where one section ends and another begins. The ribbon, platform, and gathering are different forms of the same impulse to mark a threshold. Their significance lies partly in making a change visible to others, not merely in altering a physical object.

A graduation ceremony has a comparable role. The learning recognized there took place over months or years. Walking across a platform does not create that earlier learning. It brings people together to acknowledge it. Someone unable to attend has not therefore lost the knowledge gained beforehand.
Calling such actions empty because they do not perform the underlying work overlooks their public function. A ceremony can provide a shared signal: now this place is open, or now this achievement is being recognized. Its participants can understand a transition together rather than discover it separately.
Ceremonies are punctuation in a shared story. They do not supply all the words, but they help a group recognize where one section ends and another begins. The ribbon, platform, and gathering are different forms of the same impulse to mark a threshold. Their significance lies partly in making a change visible to others, not merely in altering a physical object.
